proof:
# Local rigidity of three balanced stationary tetrahedral sections

This is a local structural theorem, not a global classification of stationary sections. It shows that a fully nonsymmetric common centroid cannot bifurcate near the rational three-section configuration already used in the exact funding theorem.

Consider three strict quadrilateral section planes of a tetrahedron, represented by raw margins c_1,c_2,c_3 with c_1+c_2+c_3=0. Near the reference configuration

    c_1=(1/5,1/2,-1,-1),
    c_2=(1/2,1/5,-1,-1),
    c_3=(-7/10,-7/10,2,2),                           (1)

suppose their actual section centroids are identical. Then their third and fourth raw coordinates agree in each row, and the common centroid has equal third and fourth coordinates. Here “near” means an open neighborhood of (1), after common positive scaling is normalized by c_14=-1. In particular no triple with four distinct common centroid coordinates exists in that neighborhood.

## 1. Explicit equations and a nonsingular Jacobian

For p,q,r,w>0, let b(p,q,r,w) be the centroid of the section with raw margins (p,q,-r,-w). Put

    X=1/p, Y=1/q, Z=1/r, W=1/w, L=X+Y+Z+W.

The actual quadrilateral centroid is given by

    3b_1=X/(X+Z)+X/(X+W)-X/L,
    3b_2=Y/(Y+Z)+Y/(Y+W)-Y/L,
    3b_3=Z/(Z+X)+Z/(Z+Y)-Z/L,
    3b_4=W/(W+X)+W/(W+Y)-W/L.                       (2)

These formulas follow from its four edge intersections and diagonal intersection; they are rational and smooth throughout the strict 2+2 cell. They are unchanged by reversing all raw margins.

Use the normalized variables

    c_1=(p,q,-r,-1),
    c_2=(u,v,-w,-z),
    c_3=(-p-u,-q-v,r+w,1+z).

Write b1=b(p,q,r,1), b2=b(u,v,w,z), and b3=b(p+u,q+v,r+w,1+z). The five equations used are

    (b1-b2)_1=(b1-b2)_2=(b1-b2)_3=0,
    (b1-b3)_1=(b1-b3)_3=0.                          (3)

Near (1), these are equivalent to equality of all three centroids. Indeed the first three give b1=b2 because coordinates sum to one. Then c_3 dot b1=0, since c_3=-c_1-c_2 and each source centroid lies in its own section. Also c_3 dot b3=0. The two remaining unknown coordinates of b1-b3 are opposite; their coefficients in c_3 are unequal near (1), since c_32=-7/10 and c_34=2 at the reference point. Hence they also vanish.

At

    (p,q,r,u,v,w,z)=(1/5,1/2,1,1/2,1/5,1,1),

the derivative matrix of (3) with respect to (r,u,v,w,z), in that order, is

    [ 25/972      44/243       50/243      -16/243       -16/243   ]
    [ 16/243      20/243       25/486      -25/972       -25/972   ]
    [-85/972     -32/243     -125/972       85/972         1/243   ]
    [  5/2916   1100/15309   1000/15309    -35/1458      -35/1458  ]
    [-739/17496  -50/729      -50/729       791/17496      49/17496].

Its determinant is exactly

    -1625/7029357352416 != 0.                        (4)

The implicit-function theorem therefore gives a unique nearby solution (r,u,v,w,z) of (3) for every nearby choice of (p,q).

## 2. An actual equal-height solution for every nearby parameter

We construct such a solution with r=1 and w=z. Fix p,q near 1/5,1/2 and let the actual centroid of (p,q,-1,-1) be (a,c,B,B). At the reference point it is (10/27,10/27,7/54,7/54), so a,c>1/3 and B>0 persist locally.

Use the actual captured-coordinate cubic F from `candidate 03420419c4771251`, equations (1)–(3). At the reference centroid it has the three simple roots

    p_1=1/5, p_2=7/20, p_3=1/2.

Thus its roots continue as smooth real functions p_1<p_2<p_3 near the reference point. The given p is p_1: its actual centroid satisfies the defining equation, and it lies near the first simple root. Put

    q_i=(2B-a p_i)/c.

Every q_i stays positive. Each (p_i,q_i,-1,-1) has the ACTUAL centroid (a,c,B,B), not merely a prescribed plane incidence. To see this, the defining equation fixes its first centroid coordinate to a. Its last two coordinates agree by the equal raw heights. Its centroid sums to one and lies in the plane. These two remaining linear equations uniquely give its second coordinate c and its two equal last coordinates B, because q_i+1>0.

Set

    lambda=(p_2-p_1)/(p_3-p_2)>0,
    r=1, u=lambda p_3, v=lambda q_3, w=z=lambda.     (5)

The normalized third representative is exactly the middle root:

    [(p_1,q_1,-1,-1)+lambda(p_3,q_3,-1,-1)]/(1+lambda)
          =(p_2,q_2,-1,-1).

The second coordinate equality follows because q is affine in p. Thus the three actual centroids in (3) agree. At the reference point lambda=1, so (5) is the nearby solution selected by the implicit-function theorem.

By uniqueness, EVERY nearby balanced triple with a common actual centroid coincides with this equal-height solution. Consequently r=1 and w=z, and all three rows have equal third/fourth raw entries. This proves the claimed local rigidity.

The argument uses a nonsingular finite-dimensional implicit system and an explicit actual-root solution. It does not claim that all stationary triples are connected to this neighborhood, that every common centroid has equal coordinates, or that the remaining nonsymmetric global strata are absent.

## 3. Rigidity near every three-root equal-central-pair configuration

The root-interpolation funding inequality proves the same local conclusion throughout its full family, including unequal first two centroid coordinates. This does not require the special determinant (4).

Fix any three distinct balanced stationary sections with common centroid (a,c,B,B), a,c>1/3. In the potentially maximizing orientation their actual margins are

    c_1=lambda_1(p_1,q_1,-1,-1),
    c_2=-lambda_2(p_2,q_2,-1,-1),
    c_3=lambda_3(p_3,q_3,-1,-1),

where p_1<p_2<p_3, all lambda_i>0, lambda_2=lambda_1+lambda_3, and the first and third sections fund the middle one. Set J_i=J(p_i)>0 and

    k_1=J_1/lambda_1, k_3=J_3/lambda_3,
    k_2=-J_2/lambda_2.

The proved exact root inequality is

    1/k_1+1/k_3 > -1/k_2.                           (6)

For any nearby balanced margins, write each row's third and fourth entries as m_i+epsilon_i,m_i-epsilon_i. Balance requires sum m_i=0 and sum epsilon_i=0. All first and second entries and the m_i may be used as the remaining parameters, subject to their linear balance equations. Choose epsilon_1,epsilon_3 as independent antisymmetric variables and set epsilon_2=-epsilon_1-epsilon_3.

Let g_i be the difference between the third and fourth coordinates of the actual centroid of row i's section. When every epsilon_i=0, every g_i is zero for EVERY nearby choice of the remaining parameters, by the coordinate-swap symmetry of the tetrahedron. At the fixed stationary configuration,

    d g_i = k_i d epsilon_i                         (7)

for antisymmetric variations. To check the coefficient, write the centroid as grad P_i/(3f_i). Its third/fourth gradient entries agree at equal raw heights, so differentiating their difference eliminates the derivative of f_i. The remaining numerator is e^T Hess(P_i)e, e=(0,0,1,-1). This gives J_i/lambda_i for the first and third orientations and its negative for the complementary middle orientation, exactly as in the actual funding formula.

The derivative of the two equations g_1-g_2=0 and g_3-g_2=0 with respect to (epsilon_1,epsilon_3) is therefore

    [[k_1+k_2, k_2],
     [k_2, k_3+k_2]].

Its determinant is

    k_1 k_3+k_2(k_1+k_3)
      =k_1 k_3[1+k_2(1/k_1+1/k_3)]<0              (8)

by (6). All section-centroid functions are smooth in this strict quadrilateral cell, as is also explicit in (2). The implicit-function theorem gives a unique small solution for the two antisymmetric variables for every nearby choice of the remaining parameters. The identically zero solution already exists for every such parameter choice. Hence it is the unique one.

Thus EVERY sufficiently close balanced triple whose actual section centroids agree must retain equal third and fourth raw heights in each row, and its common centroid retains equal third and fourth coordinates. The same conclusion holds if all three orientations are reversed, since the section-centroid equations are unoriented and their zero sets do not change.

This proves local rigidity along the whole three-root family. It rules out a nonsymmetric bifurcation there. It does not rule out distant nonsymmetric solution components, limits where roots collide, or a different incidence split.
